newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: High yen to provide relief to S.Korean car industry.
newsitem.headline: High yen to provide relief to S.Korean car industry.

text.p: A stronger yen would boost South Korea's car industry, analysts said, but one company official warned against underestimating Japan's ability to compete.
"Exports will certainly get a boost from the rising yen, albeit after a six-month lag time," said Chang Choon-rin, an analyst at Daewoo Research Institute.
"The yen's rise against the dollar must be a blessing to South Korean carmakers who are suffering from faltering domestic sales."

Domestic sales in April by Hyundai Motor Co were flat, while sales by Kia Motors Corp plunged 20 percent. However, Daewoo Motor Co, a unit of the Daewoo Group, saw its home sales surge 50 percent on demand for new models.
With inventories rising, Korean car makers introduced a range of incentives in April, including non-interest instalment payment schemes, to boost domestic sales.
Analysts said car makers have been distorting sales figures to hide slackening demand at home and abroad.
"Their sales at home were inflated by about 15 percent as they count sales on an ex-factory basis," said Kim Myung-joon, analyst at Dongwon Economic Research Institute.
With many cars sitting idle in parking lots of carmakers' outlets, the Korea Automobile Manufacturers' Association decided to release sales figures on the basis of registration by car owners.
Analysts said the yen would creep up for the time being in the view that it was still undervalued.
The yen was quoted in Tokyo at 116.46/50 per dollar at mid-morning on Friday, up from the year's low of 127.45 on May 1.
"We set our export target for this year at 450,000 units. Now we expect more," said Chung Phil-kyong, director of Kia Motors Corp's export division.
Kim Noi-myung, executive managing director of Hyundai Motor, the largest carmaker, said: "Japanese car makers will have to cut incentives to their overseas dealers. That much will help us."
Hyundai Motor aimed to export 670,000 units this year, compared with 570,000 units last year.
"We don't plan to revise our earlier export target. The effect of the rising yen will be felt more strongly next year," Kim said.

South Korean cars sold overseas were about 20 percent cheaper than their Japanese counterparts. But analysts said South Korean cars would not become truly competitive against their Japanese rivals until the price difference reached 25 percent.
"The yen should rise above 110, then prices of South Korean cars will be optimal," said Nam Seung-soo, an analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute.
But one Korean executive warned that Korean car makers should not underestimate Japan's ability to compete despite the yen's strength.
"Japanese producers can survive even at the yen's rate of 80/90 per dollar because of their past restructuring," said Kim Sun-chang, general managing director of Daewoo Motor.
"Advantageous pricing will help. But the real competitiveness should come from quality," he said.
